problem:
Suppose that for the angles $u$ and $v,$ we have

$$
\operatorname{sin}⁡u=\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2},\,\operatorname{cos}⁡v=\frac{12}{15},\,\operatorname{sin}⁡v=\frac{9}{15}.
$$

Given that $u$ lies in the second quadrant, find the value of $\operatorname{cos}⁡(u+v).$
worked_solution:
First, we recall the sum formula for cosine:

$$
\operatorname{cos}⁡(u+v)=\operatorname{cos}⁡u\operatorname{cos}⁡v-\operatorname{sin}⁡u\operatorname{sin}⁡v
$$

We know the values of $\operatorname{sin}⁡u,$ $\operatorname{cos}⁡v,$ and $\operatorname{sin}⁡v.$ To find the missing value of $\operatorname{cos}⁡u,$ we can use the Pythagorean identity:

$$
{sin}^{2}⁡u+{cos}^{2}⁡u=1\,⟹\,{cos}^{2}⁡u=1-{sin}^{2}⁡u
$$

Substituting our values into the Pythagorean identity, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{cos}^{2}⁡u & =1-{sin}^{2}⁡u \\  & =1-{(\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2})}^{2} \\  & =1-\frac{(\sqrt{2})^{2}}{{2}^{2}} \\  & =1-\frac{2}{4} \\  & =\frac{4}{4}-\frac{2}{4} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡u & =\pm \sqrt{\frac{1}{2}} \\  & =\pm \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

We're given that $u$ lies in the second quadrant, where cosine is negative. So, we disregard the positive value, and we have

$$
\operatorname{cos}⁡u=-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}.
$$

We can now apply the sum formula:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(u+v) & =\operatorname{cos}⁡u\operatorname{cos}⁡v-\operatorname{sin}⁡u\operatorname{sin}⁡v \\  & =(-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2})(\frac{12}{15})-(\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2})(\frac{9}{15}) \\  & =-\frac{12\sqrt{2}}{30}-\frac{9\sqrt{2}}{30} \\  & =-\frac{21\sqrt{2}}{30} \\  & =-\frac{7\sqrt{2}}{10}\end{aligned}
$$
